notes.meaning: The tribe of Dan gave four cities to the Kohathite clans who were not priests. These towns sat in Dan's territory in the southwestern plains near the coast. God ensured that even tribes facing tough border conflicts shared their towns to support His ministers.

The half-tribe of Manasseh living west of the Jordan River gave two cities, bringing the total for the remaining Kohathite families to ten cities. These Levites had the special duty of caring for the sacred furnishings of the tabernacle. Placing them in central Israel kept them close to the sanctuary where they would serve.

The Gershonite Levites received two cities from the eastern half-tribe of Manasseh across the Jordan. Golan was set apart as a city of refuge to protect anyone who caused an accidental death. Beeshterah had once been a center for worshipping a Canaanite goddess, but God turned it into a home for His ministers.

Four cities from the tribe of Issachar were given to the Gershonite clans. These towns were located in the fertile valley of Jezreel. Here the Levites could live and provide spiritual guidance to the families around them.

The Gershonites were also given four cities from the territory of Asher in northwestern Canaan. This ensured that even distant coastal communities had spiritual leaders close at hand. God arranged the towns so that every corner of the nation had access to His word.

Naphtali provided three cities to the Gershonites, including Kedesh in Galilee, which served as a city of refuge for northern Israel. In all, the Gershonite clans received thirteen cities across the northern and eastern regions. These towns provided homes for the Levites who were responsible for carrying the tabernacle's curtains and coverings.

The Merarites, the last family branch of Levi, received four cities from the tribe of Zebulun. Merari was the youngest son of Levi, and his clan carried the heavy wooden frames and pillars of the tabernacle. God provided them an inheritance among their brothers just as He had for the older clans.

The tribe of Reuben on the east side of the Jordan provided four cities to the Merarites. One of these was Bezer, a city of refuge located out on the flat desert plateau. Although a few ancient Hebrew copies skipped these verses by a copyist mistake, ancient translations and the best manuscripts preserve them to complete the count of twelve Merarite cities.

The Merarites received four cities from the tribe of Gad, including the city of refuge at Ramoth in Gilead and the town of Mahanaim. Mahanaim was a famous place where Jacob had once met God's angels, and it later gave shelter to King David. These homes placed faithful ministers right along Israel's eastern border.
The Merarite clans received twelve cities in total from the tribes of Zebulun, Reuben, and Gad. This completed the specific distribution of towns to all three main branches of the tribe of Levi.

Altogether, forty-eight cities with their surrounding pasturelands were set apart for the Levites throughout Israel. The open fields around each town gave them space to feed their livestock and grow food alongside the tithes they received. Scattering the Levites across the nation gave every tribe nearby teachers to help them know and obey God's law.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: The list of forty-eight Levitical cities is viewed as an idealized account written in later centuries when the priesthood was fully established, rather than an exact record of the conquest era.

notes.meaning: The Lord gave Israel the entire land He had sworn to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob centuries before. The tribes took possession of Canaan and settled down in their new homes. Even though some Canaanite pockets remained, Israel held full authority over the land and occupied as much as they needed at that time.

The Lord gave the people rest from the hard march through the wilderness and the strain of war. Not a single enemy could stand against them, because God delivered all their opponents into their hands. The remaining Canaanites were so broken by fear that they could no longer mount an attack while Joshua and his generation lived.

Every single good promise the Lord had spoken to the house of Israel came completely true. This summary gives all the glory to God for keeping His covenant from start to finish. It assures believers that God's word never fails and that He can be trusted completely.

differ.view: God fulfilled His promises completely on His part, and any land left unconquered was caused entirely by Israel's own laziness and lack of courage.
God proved entirely faithful to His word, but the people's ongoing possession of the land remained conditional on their continued obedience.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: This passage reflects an idealized summary from a later priestly editor, contrasting with older accounts that describe a much slower and partial conquest.
